deed: הרב אברהם יהושע השל צועד בסלמה לצד מרטין לותר קינג
title: Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel marched in Selma alongside Martin Luther King for voting rights

trailer.text: Abraham Joshua Heschel was a Jewish theologian and philosopher, and his social consciousness led him to participate in the civil rights movement.
He was born in 1907 in Warsaw, and lost his mother and three of his sisters in the Holocaust.
In March 1965, Heschel responded to Martin Luther King’s call for religious leaders and joined the Selma to Montgomery March for voting rights.
When he returned, he said that for many the march was protest and prayer, and that he felt his feet were praying.
After the march, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, and the president signed it.

paragraphs.text: Heschel was born in 1907 in Warsaw, Poland, to Rabbi Moshe Mordecai and Reizel Perlow Heschel.
He was born to a Chasidic family, and was named after his great-great-grandfather, the Apter Rav.
He taught in Warsaw and London.
In 1940 he emigrated to the United States.

According to a review of the biography written by Julian Zelizer, Heschel left Germany only a few months before the outbreak of the war, thanks to the offer of a fellowship at the Reform Hebrew Union College in Cincinnati, Ohio.
His daughter Susannah wrote that he arrived as a refugee from Nazi Europe.
There, many Christian theologians were declaring Jesus an Aryan, not a Jew.
Heschel lost his mother and three of his sisters in the Holocaust.
In 1943, Heschel took part in a rabbis’ march in Washington.
The march was meant to press the United States government to do more for Jews abroad.
According to a historian, a delegation of about 400 rabbis marched in this march.
According to PBS, Heschel also campaigned for the rights of Jews in the Soviet Union.
According to PBS, he also lobbied hard at the Second Vatican Council against church teachings that demeaned Jews.

stations.title: Chicago 1963: the rabbi and the minister meet

paragraphs.text: According to the King Institute at Stanford, on 14 January 1963 Heschel gave the opening address at the National Conference on Religion and Race in Chicago, and King also spoke there.
Heschel said in the speech that “the Negro problem” is God’s gift to America.
In his words, it is a test of America’s integrity and a magnificent spiritual opportunity.
Heschel set out to fight racism, and he called racism “satanism”.
According to Susannah Heschel, when Heschel and King met in 1963 they felt an instant bond, despite great differences in their backgrounds.
In November 1963, King expressed deep accord with Heschel’s struggle against the Soviet Union’s treatment of its Jews.
According to Susannah Heschel, at home they saw on television peaceful black demonstrators who were treated cruelly, with vicious dogs and water hoses.
According to Susannah Heschel, on Friday afternoon a telegram arrived for the family inviting her father to the march in Selma.
In March 1965, Heschel responded to King’s call for religious leaders to join the Selma to Montgomery March for voting rights.
According to historian Julian Zelizer, Heschel did not go to the first march in Selma but to the last one, a few weeks later.
President Lyndon Johnson had just declared “We Shall Overcome,” and congressional passage of the Voting Rights Act was expected to come quickly.
According to Susannah Heschel, when her father came to Selma, he and others slept at the Jackson family home.

According to Susannah Heschel, Mrs. Jackson told her that on the morning of the march she saw King, her father Rabbi Heschel and a priest in the living room of her home, each praying in his own way in a different corner of the room, and they all said psalms just before the march began.
According to her, just before the march began, they all said psalms.
The famous photograph was taken at the March on Selma on March 21, 1965.
It shows Heschel and King wearing Hawaiian leis.
According to Susannah Heschel, the march was not like “Bloody Sunday” a few weeks earlier, and was not a moment of terror.
According to her, it was both a political protest and a deeply religious moment.
According to her, it brought together nuns, priests and rabbis from all over the United States.
According to Susannah Heschel, walking across the Edmund Pettus Bridge, named for a Confederate general, invited all Americans to unite against segregation and racism.
According to Susannah Heschel, Andrew Young told her that many activists carried in their pockets a copy of Heschel’s book on the prophets.
Heschel saved accounts written by rabbis and laypeople who had also answered King's call to come to Selma, and these accounts are now part of the Heschel collection at Duke University.
Barbara Krasner, a mother of five, went to Selma even though women were told it was better not to come.
According to Rabbi Teitelbaum’s diary, the rabbis held a Sabbath service in Selma and closed by singing Adon Olam to the melody of “We Shall Overcome.”
According to a rabbi who took part in the march, the kippah became a mark of distinction there and a sought-after item, and Black people called it a ‘freedom cap’.
According to Susannah Heschel, her father said that King told him it was the greatest day in his life.
When he returned, Heschel said that for many the march was protest and prayer.
Heschel's statement that he felt his legs were praying is sometimes misquoted as “praying with his feet.”
After the march, Congress passed the Voting Rights Act, and the president signed it.
According to Susannah Heschel, through his friendship with her father, King spoke out forcefully on behalf of Soviet Jews, in support of the State of Israel and against the war in Vietnam.
On 4 April 1967, King spoke against the Vietnam War at Riverside Church, and Heschel spoke after him.
Heschel was among the first prominent Americans to speak out publicly against United States involvement in the war in Southeast Asia.
In a meeting with Henry Kissinger, Heschel asked him how he, as a good Jew, could prosecute such a war.
After the Six-Day War, Heschel defended Israel against radicals who accused it of being an outcrop of the imperialist West.
In March 1968, King entered the hall of the Rabbinical Assembly convention.
The rabbis stood up, linked arms and sang “We Shall Overcome” in Hebrew in his honor.

In the conversation with Martin Luther King, published in spring 1968 in the journal Conservative Judaism, King said that Rabbi Heschel is one of the persons who is relevant at all times, always standing with prophetic insights.
According to Susannah Heschel, her father read a psalm at King's funeral, in spring 1968.
Heschel died on December 23, 1972, at the age of 65.
At the time of his death, he was one of the most prominent Jewish figures in the United States.
According to PBS, he is considered one of the greatest American religious figures of the last century, and was esteemed by Christians as well as by Jews.
According to Susannah Heschel, President Barack Obama quoted on several occasions what Heschel said when he returned from Selma.
In 2020, a photograph of Heschel and King together appeared at the center of an advertisement in the Senate campaign of Raphael Warnock and Jon Ossoff, who is Jewish.
According to Professor Eric Meyers of Duke, the participation of many Jews in the civil rights movement shaped an entire generation of American Jews.

stations.title: Those who stayed out of the picture

paragraphs.text: According to Susannah Heschel, many Jews said that Jews should care only about Jews and not get involved in the civil rights movement.
According to Susannah Heschel, her father’s colleagues at the seminary did not join him in Selma.
According to Susannah Heschel, the New York Times printed the photograph the next day and cut her father out of it.
Years later she wrote that it was a pity her father’s presence is not included in the film “Selma.”

unknowns.text: In the iconic photograph from the March on Selma on March 21, 1965, marching from left to right: John Lewis, an unidentified nun, Ralph Abernathy, Martin Luther King Jr., Ralph Bunche, Abraham Joshua Heschel and Reverend Fred Shuttlesworth.

In March 1965, Heschel responded to King’s call for religious leaders to join the Selma to Montgomery March for voting rights. For him the march was a fulfilling spiritual experience, and he said that when he marched alongside King he felt that his feet were praying.

claims.text: לפי פרופסור אריק מאיירס מדיוק, השתתפות יהודים רבים בתנועה לזכויות האזרח עיצבה דור שלם של יהודים אמריקאים.
claims.quote: The participation of so many Jews in the civil rights movement was formative for an entire generation of American Jews.

claims.text: לפי סוזנה השל, יהודים רבים אמרו שיהודים צריכים לדאוג רק ליהודים אחרים ולא להתערב בתנועה לזכויות האזרח.
claims.quote: there were a lot of Jews who said, for example, that Jews should only be concerned about other Jews, don’t get involved in the Civil Rights Movement

claims.text: לפי סוזנה השל, עמיתיו של אביה בסמינר לא הצטרפו אליו לסלמה.
claims.quote: His colleagues at the seminary didn’t go with him to Selma.

claims.text: לפי סוזנה השל, הניו יורק טיימס פרסם למחרת את התצלום בלי אביה, כלומר גזר אותו החוצה.
claims.quote: the New York Times printed the photograph without my father. They cut him out.

claims.text: סוזנה השל כתבה שחבל שנוכחותו של אביה אינה נכללת בסרט "Selma".
claims.quote: What a pity that my father’s presence is not included in “Selma.”

claims.text: לפי אתר אוניברסיטת ברנדייס, כשהצטרף לקינג בצעדה ב-1965 אמר השל שהרגיש שהוא מתפלל ברגליו.
claims.quote: When he joined King in the 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery for voting rights, Heschel said he felt like he was

claims.text: לפי אחד המקורות, בסוף ההפגנה שאל עיתונאי את השל על רגשותיו, והוא ענה: "הרגליים שלי התפללו".
claims.quote: At the end of the demonstration, a journalist asked Heschel to describe his feelings about marching with King.

claims.text: לפי PBS, השל הצליח לברוח מאירופה כשישה שבועות בלבד לפני מלחמת העולם השנייה.
claims.quote: Just six weeks before World War II, he was able to escape from Europe.

claims.text: לפי ראיון עם ההיסטוריון ג'וליאן זליצר, בינואר 1963 הזמין קינג את השל לדבר בכנס על דת וגזע בשיקגו.
claims.quote: And then in January 1963, King invited Heschel to be a speaker at a conference on religion and race in Chicago.

claims.text: לפי סוזנה השל, הכנס על דת וגזע בשיקגו, שבו פגש השל את קינג לראשונה, אורגן בידי הוועידה הלאומית של נוצרים ויהודים.
claims.quote: My father went to Chicago to give a speech at a conference on religion and race that had been organized by the National Conference of Christians and Jews.
